name: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS, BASS-II)
objective: Flame spread vs. O2 and flow

name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME, SAME-R)
objective: Measure the size distribution of smoke from overheated (pyrolyzing, not flaming) spacecraft materials in microgravity, so spacecraft smoke detectors can be designed from low-g data instead of 1 g data
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the ISS: heated-wire smoke generation duct, piston aging chamber, diagnostics duct with moment instruments, ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors, thermal precipitator for TEM grids

fuel.shape: small sample heated by a wire coil below its ignition point for about 60 s
fuel.size: sized for 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 s at the baseline temperature

diluents: N2 (ISS cabin air; O2 and pressure are cabin nominal, not stated in the papers)

varied: air flow past the sample (baseline 8 cm/s, down to 2 cm/s, plus 11 quiescent tests)
sensors: P-Trak condensation nuclei counter (zeroth moment, 20 nm to 1 µm)
ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector (first moment)
DustTrak light scattering (third moment, 1 µm and 10 µm impactors)
MPASS two-angle scattering sensor, a prototype two-moment detector (SAME-2)
ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors
key_findings: Most average smoke particle sizes were 200 to 400 nm; quiescent cases sometimes produced much larger particles.
Unaged diameter of average mass ranged from 101 nm (Kapton) to 465 nm (silicone); after 720 s of aging it ranged from 161 nm to 619 nm.
Teflon and Kapton smoke was very small, which makes it hard for light-scattering detectors like the ISS detector to see.
Diameter of average mass was 30 to 40% larger in zero-flow tests than in flow tests, so smoke trapped in an enclosure is larger than smoke in ventilated areas.
The two-moment MPASS sensor cut the relative variance of its response by at least a factor of 2 versus a single-output sensor, which can separate a lot of smoke from a little large dust.
Across materials, the diameter of average mass increased on average by a factor of 1.7 in low gravity.
sources: Yang et al., Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), NASA TM 2010, NIST pub 904707

name: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT, DAFT-2)
objective: Check that the P-Trak particle counter (a key SAME instrument) works in long-duration microgravity, and make the first measurement of background particle levels in ISS cabin air
hardware: Hand-held TSI P-Trak condensation nuclei counter (modified condenser grooves for low-g condensate return) and TSI DustTrak, plus a reference dust source on the later flight

fuel.size: P-Trak counts particles down to 20 nm

varied: aerosol source (undisturbed air, Velcro separation, reference dust)
key_findings: ISS cabin air averaged below 0.005 mg/m3 (DustTrak) and below 15 particles/cm3 (P-Trak), substantially cleaner than the Space Shuttle or a typical office.
Deliberately separating Velcro produced a large transient particle spike, a nuisance source a smoke detector must not alarm on.
The modified P-Trak worked in low gravity; reference-dust readings agreed with the DustTrak on the first run before low alcohol degraded it.
DAFT was flown on Expedition 10 (P-Trak and DustTrak) and Expedition 13 (reference source).

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
objective: Study droplet combustion and extinction, including suppression by diluents
hardware: MDCA in the Combustion Integrated Rack
key_findings: Cool flame burning after visible extinction for large heptane droplets

name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
objective: Six independent studies of non-premixed gaseous flames in the Combustion Integrated Rack; the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) study targets spacecraft fire prevention by studying material flammability in still air
hardware: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), about 83 L free volume, constant-volume tests; gas-jet, coflow, spherical and BRE porous burners

fuel.shape: gas-jet, coflow, porous spherical and flat porous (BRE) burners
fuel.size: BRE porous burners 25 mm (ethylene, methane) and 50 mm (ethylene) diameter

varied: ambient O2 mole fraction (BRE nominal 0.21, 0.265, 0.34, 0.40; measured 0.18 to 0.39)
burner size (BRE 25 mm and 50 mm; methane on 25 mm only)
electric field (E-FIELD Flames, up to 10 kV)
held_constant: still chamber atmosphere for BRE (no forced flow)
sensors: heat flux gauges and slug calorimeter (BRE)
intensified OH* and CH* / formaldehyde cameras
key_findings: BRE flames self-extinguished in O2 below about 25% by volume; in 21% O2 all 25 mm ethylene flames went out within 40 s, while steady flames were seen at 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2.
BRE ran flames at 10.2 psia (70 kPa), the planned Moon base and rover pressure, at O2 0.24 to 0.29.
Larger BRE flames generally self-extinguished within 1.5 minutes; methane flames went out within a minute while ethylene flames at elevated O2 burned for minutes.
BRE extinction times decreased with burner diameter and did not depend on pressure (8.2 to 14.7 psia).
The results support significant fire hazards for enriched-oxygen spacecraft atmospheres.
CFI-G observed non-premixed cool flames with n-butane on porous burners.
sources: hdl:1903/27484 (Wright, UMD thesis, 2021; Appendix B test tables)
